questions.prompt: Why should API data be validated at the boundary before it enters application state?

options.text: External data may be missing, malformed, or have the wrong types
JSON guarantees the application's expected schema
The browser validates business rules automatically
Validation makes asynchronous work parallel

questions.explanation: Parsing establishes syntax, not the application schema; validate assumptions where data enters the system.

questions.prompt: Which test checks whether a number is within JavaScript's safe integer range?

options.text: `Number.isIntegerSafe(value)`
`Number.isSafeInteger(value)`
`value === parseInt(value)`
`typeof value === 'integer'`

questions.explanation: Safe integers are exactly representable and can be tested with `Number.isSafeInteger`.

questions.prompt: Which practices make async workflows more reliable?

options.text: Return or await Promises whose failures matter.
Use cancellation or stale-result checks for obsolete work.
Bound concurrency for large workloads.
Assume `Promise.all` cancels siblings after rejection.

questions.explanation: `Promise.all` rejects as an aggregate but does not cancel already-started operations.

questions.prompt: Why can `try { save(); } catch { ... }` miss a later rejection from `save()`?

options.text: Try/catch cannot catch any Promise
Promises disable thrown errors
The Promise rejection happens after the synchronous try block has finished
The catch block only handles strings

questions.explanation: Await the Promise inside the try or attach a rejection handler so the failure is observed.

questions.prompt: Match each failure symptom to a suitable engineering response.

rows.label: Old search response overwrites new results

columns.label: Move suitable CPU work off main thread

questions.explanation: Prevent stale updates, inspect HTTP status, and isolate CPU-bound work where appropriate.

questions.prompt: If one Promise passed to `Promise.all` rejects, what happens to other operations already started?

options.text: All other Promises are canceled automatically
The aggregate waits and then fulfills
The other Promises are converted to `undefined`
The aggregate rejects, but the other operations are not automatically canceled

questions.explanation: `Promise.all` aggregates outcomes; it has no built-in cancellation mechanism.

questions.prompt: What is a risk of starting thousands of independent requests at once with `Promise.all`?

options.text: Unbounded concurrency can exhaust resources or overload a service
`Promise.all` serializes all requests
Promises require a separate thread each
It changes the result order randomly

questions.explanation: A concurrency limit or work queue can bound resource use while preserving parallelism.

questions.prompt: Which practices reduce DOM injection risk?

options.text: Concatenate untrusted values into `innerHTML`.
Use `textContent` for untrusted text.
Build nodes with DOM methods.
Validate data before using it in application logic.

questions.explanation: Treat untrusted values as text and validate their shape; do not parse them as markup.

questions.prompt: A user starts search A, then search B; A returns last and overwrites B. Which approach addresses stale requests?

options.text: Use `Promise.race` without tracking requests
Abort the prior request or ignore results from outdated request IDs
Make the result object `const`
Put the search field in a closure

questions.explanation: Cancellation or request-version checks prevent old responses from overwriting newer state.

questions.prompt: Which DOM API should render untrusted user text as text rather than parsed markup?

options.text: `innerHTML` with direct concatenation
`document.write`
`textContent`
`outerHTML`

questions.explanation: `textContent` avoids interpreting user-provided strings as HTML.

questions.prompt: Match each Promise outcome pattern to its combinator.
questions.explanation: Choose a combinator based on required fulfillment and rejection behavior.

questions.prompt: In event delegation, why might a handler use `event.target.closest('button')`?

options.text: `currentTarget` always points to the deepest nested element
`closest()` cancels the event
The browser does not bubble click events
The original target may be a nested element inside the button

questions.explanation: A click can originate on an icon or span inside a control; `closest` finds the intended ancestor.

questions.prompt: What is a benefit of abortable event listeners using an `AbortSignal`?

options.text: A group of listeners can be removed when their controller is aborted
It makes every event handler run in parallel
It prevents default actions automatically
It serializes listener options

questions.explanation: Passing a signal to `addEventListener` supports lifecycle cleanup by aborting its controller.

questions.prompt: Which practices support responsive browser performance?

options.text: Move suitable CPU-heavy work to a Worker.
Assume a Promise makes CPU work parallel.
Measure before optimizing.
Batch related DOM reads and writes.

questions.explanation: Promises schedule asynchronous completion but execute JavaScript callbacks on the same thread.

questions.prompt: Why can repeated DOM reads and writes in alternating order be expensive?

options.text: The DOM stores only one element
They can force repeated style/layout calculations
JavaScript automatically moves the work to a worker
Every write always triggers a network request

questions.explanation: Layout-dependent reads after writes may force synchronous rendering work; batch reads and writes where practical.

questions.prompt: Match each JavaScript scheduling source to its effect.

columns.label: Prevents other work on that thread until completion

questions.explanation: Synchronous work blocks its agent; microtasks and tasks have different queue positions; Workers use another agent.

questions.prompt: Where should CPU-intensive computation run if it would block a responsive browser main thread?

options.text: In a Promise callback on the same thread
In a `queueMicrotask` callback
In a Worker when the data and API requirements permit
Inside a CSS animation

questions.explanation: Promises and microtasks do not create threads; workers provide a separate execution context for CPU work.

questions.prompt: What happens to an ArrayBuffer after it is transferred to a Worker?

options.text: The sender and receiver share the same ordinary buffer
The bytes are converted to a string
The Worker receives only a copy of the first byte
The sender's buffer is detached and ownership moves to the receiver

questions.explanation: Transferables move ownership without copying; the sender can no longer use the transferred buffer.

questions.prompt: Which statements about JavaScript memory and immutability are correct?

options.text: Closures can keep captured bindings reachable.
Event listeners can retain referenced state until removed.
`const` deeply freezes an object.
`Object.freeze` is shallow.

questions.explanation: Reachability determines garbage collection; `const` constrains a binding, and freeze is shallow.

questions.prompt: Why can recursively queuing microtasks make an interface unresponsive?

options.text: The microtask queue may keep draining before tasks or rendering get a turn
Microtasks always run on a different CPU
They cancel the JavaScript call stack
They are delayed until after all timers

questions.explanation: A self-perpetuating microtask chain can starve later tasks and browser rendering opportunities.

questions.prompt: Which data structure is appropriate for private metadata keyed by object identity without making keys enumerable?

options.text: `Array`
`WeakMap`
`JSON`
`WeakSet` with string keys

questions.explanation: WeakMap accepts object keys and does not expose key enumeration, avoiding a strong key-retention relationship.

questions.prompt: Match each copy or lifecycle operation to its guarantee.

columns.label: Copies own enumerable properties one level
Prevents direct changes to that object
Does not make the key enumerable/strongly retained

questions.explanation: These operations have limited but useful guarantees; none automatically deep-clones an object graph.

questions.prompt: What does `Object.freeze(config)` guarantee about nested objects?

options.text: Every nested value is deeply immutable
It serializes the object
It does not recursively freeze them
It prevents reading any property

questions.explanation: `Object.freeze` is shallow; nested objects need separate handling if deep immutability is required.

questions.prompt: Why are ES module cycles worth reviewing during refactoring?

options.text: Cycles are always syntax errors
Cycles automatically duplicate every module
Static imports execute only when a function is called
A module can access another module's live binding before initialization completes

questions.explanation: Cycles are legal, but initialization order and live bindings can expose uninitialized values.

questions.prompt: Which statements about event-loop scheduling are correct?

options.text: A long synchronous task blocks the current thread.
Promise reactions are microtasks.
A self-sustaining microtask chain can delay rendering.
`queueMicrotask` creates a worker thread.

questions.explanation: Microtasks run on the same JavaScript agent and can delay subsequent tasks.

questions.prompt: Why is `toSorted()` useful when updating state from an existing array?

options.text: It creates a sorted copy instead of mutating the shared source
It deeply clones every item
It guarantees numeric order without a comparator
It removes duplicate values

questions.explanation: Non-mutating updates reduce accidental changes to shared state; numeric sorting still needs a comparator.

questions.prompt: Match each input-handling technique to its purpose.

columns.label: Insert text without parsing it as markup
Parse JSON grammar and may throw

questions.explanation: Safe input handling separates text rendering, syntax parsing, and domain validation.

questions.prompt: Which check rejects both `NaN` and positive/negative infinity?

options.text: `Boolean(value)`
`Number.isFinite(value)`
`value !== null`
`Number.isInteger(value)`

questions.explanation: `Number.isFinite` checks that the value is a finite Number without coercing other types.

questions.prompt: Why should a catch handler not assume every caught value is an `Error` instance?

options.text: Only strings can be thrown
Promises turn all errors into numbers
JavaScript permits throwing any value
Catch bindings are always `null`

questions.explanation: Any JavaScript value can be thrown, so normalize or validate the caught value before reading Error-specific fields.

questions.prompt: Which practices improve error observability?

options.text: Silently replace failures with success-shaped defaults.
Preserve a lower-level error as `cause` when wrapping it.
Handle rejected event-handler Promises explicitly.
Validate caught values before assuming Error fields.

questions.explanation: Preserving causes and surfacing failures makes diagnosis reliable; silent fallback can conceal broken behavior.

questions.prompt: What is a useful practice when adding context to a lower-level failure?

options.text: Discard the original error and return `undefined`
Log the error and continue as if successful
Replace the error with a random string
Throw a higher-level error with the original error as `cause`

questions.explanation: Error causes preserve the underlying failure while adding domain context.

questions.prompt: How can a component avoid processing a response after it has been disposed?

options.text: Abort its request or check a lifecycle/request token before updating state
Set the Promise to `null`
Call `preventDefault()` on the response
Change the variable from `let` to `const`

questions.explanation: Tie asynchronous work to component lifetime and reject stale completion before state changes.

questions.prompt: Match each runtime ownership choice to its consequence.

columns.label: Sender no longer owns/uses that buffer
May remain reachable while closure is reachable

questions.explanation: `const` does not freeze object contents; transfer moves ownership; closures retain reachable environments.

questions.prompt: Which test design makes time-dependent behavior easier to reproduce?

options.text: Wait an arbitrary long time in every test
Inject a clock or timer boundary that tests can control
Use the real network
Depend on the current date without asserting it

questions.explanation: Controllable dependencies make scheduling and time conditions deterministic.

questions.prompt: Which statements about shallow copies are correct?

options.text: Object spread copies own enumerable properties.
Spread recursively freezes nested values.
Nested object references can remain shared.
A copied array can still contain shared objects.

questions.explanation: Spread copies one level and does not deep-clone or freeze nested references.

questions.prompt: Why can module-level side effects make a module harder to test?

options.text: ES modules cannot export functions
Side effects are always asynchronous
Importing it may perform work before a test can configure dependencies
The module scope is shared with every file

questions.explanation: Keep initialization explicit when possible so dependencies and effects can be controlled.

questions.prompt: Which architecture best improves first-load resilience for a browser application?

options.text: Require JavaScript before any content exists
Hide all content until every API request completes
Place essential labels only in CSS pseudo-elements
Render meaningful HTML first and enhance behavior after JavaScript loads

questions.explanation: Progressive enhancement keeps core content accessible while client behavior initializes.

questions.prompt: Which Worker statements are correct?

options.text: Workers provide a separate execution context.
Workers are useful for suitable CPU-bound work.
A Worker callback can directly manipulate the page DOM.
Transferables can move buffer ownership.

questions.explanation: Workers communicate by messages; DOM access is generally restricted to the main thread.

questions.prompt: What can happen when an `async` event handler rejects and nobody observes its returned Promise?

options.text: The rejection may become unhandled
The browser automatically retries the handler
The handler's Promise is silently fulfilled
The click event is canceled

questions.explanation: Event dispatch does not automatically await a handler's returned Promise; handle asynchronous failures explicitly.

questions.prompt: Why should a hot CPU loop not be 'yielded' only with repeated `await Promise.resolve()`?

options.text: `await` always blocks the main thread forever
It can keep scheduling microtasks and still starve tasks and rendering
Promise resolution moves the loop into a Worker
It changes arithmetic precision

questions.explanation: Yielding to a future task or using a Worker may be needed; microtask checkpoints can be starved by continually added microtasks.

questions.prompt: Which practices support maintainable module and test boundaries?

options.text: Keep side effects explicit where possible.
Inject clocks or external services for deterministic tests.
Break fragile module cycles when practical.
Make every dependency a global variable.

questions.explanation: Explicit dependencies and controlled effects improve testability and simplify initialization.

questions.prompt: Which design reduces accidental mutation when several consumers share a list of records?

options.text: Use `const` and assume all nested data is frozen
Sort the shared array in place
Return a new array for updates and document whether record objects are also shared
Store the list in a global variable

questions.explanation: Array copies protect list order, but shallow copies still share record references; define the ownership boundary.
